title: Pagination
subtitle: Why Offset/Limit pagination breaks at scale, and how Keyset/Cursor pagination guarantees O(1) index seeking.
keyTakeaways: Offset pagination (`OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20`) forces relational database engines to scan and discard 100,000 index rows, causing query latency to spike linearly with page depth.
Offset pagination suffers from page drift: if a new row is inserted while a user navigates between pages, they will observe duplicate items on the next page.
Keyset (Cursor) pagination uses indexed ordering columns (`WHERE (created_at, id) < ($cursor_time, $cursor_id)`) to seek directly to the next page in O(1) time.
architectureDiagram:
PAGINATION MECHANICS: OFFSET VS CURSOR
OFFSET PAGINATION (Linear O(N) Scan Overhead):
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000;
[ Disk Read ] -> Reads and discards 500,000 rows -> Returns 20 rows (Slow! High IOPS)

CURSOR PAGINATION (Direct O(log N) B-Tree Seek):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-01', 9942) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
[ B-Tree Index ] -> Jumps straight to leaf pointer -> Reads 20 rows immediately (Sub-5ms!)

sections.heading: The Two Fatal Flaws of Offset Pagination at Scale
sections.body: Offset pagination (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000`) is simple to implement and maps cleanly to UI pagination controls ('Jump to Page 500'). However, in production databases, it introduces two severe failure modes.
bullets: Linear Performance Collapse: Databases cannot jump directly to row 100,000 on disk. The storage engine must traverse the B-Tree index, fetch 100,020 rows, discard the first 100,000 in memory, and return the remaining 20. On tables with millions of rows, deep pages take seconds to execute and saturate database IOPS.

Page Drift / Data Inconsistency: If an infinite-scroll mobile feed uses offset pagination and 5 new posts are published while the user views page 1, requesting page 2 (`OFFSET 20`) causes the last 5 posts from page 1 to shift down into page 2, presenting the user with duplicate records.

sections.heading: Engineering Bulletproof Cursor Pagination
sections.body: Cursor pagination works by pointing to a specific record and asking the database for items that occur strictly before or after that point. By anchoring queries on an indexed column (or composite key), the database performs a sub-millisecond B-Tree index seek regardless of whether you are on the 1st page or the 10,000th page.
bullets: Tie-Breaking with Unique Columns: Timestamps alone are not unique; multiple records created in the same millisecond cause skipping or duplicates. Always use a composite cursor: `(created_at, id)`.
Opaque Cursors: Never expose raw database column values directly in client API contracts. Base64-encode or encrypt cursor payloads so client code treats the cursor as an opaque token.

The Usability Trade-off: Cursor pagination does not support jumping directly to arbitrary pages ('Go to Page 42') or calculating total pages. It is specifically optimized for infinite scroll feeds, chat histories, and export streams.

tradeOffs.pros: Trivial to implement in SQL; allows jumping directly to arbitrary page numbers; supports total page counts.
tradeOffs.cons: O(N) database latency on deep pages; causes duplicate items and missed items during active concurrent writes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal admin panels with small datasets (<10,000 rows) requiring direct page jump navigation.

tradeOffs.pros: Deterministic O(1) performance regardless of table depth; completely immune to page drift and duplicate items.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot jump directly to arbitrary page numbers; sorting requires matching composite database indexes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-scale public APIs, social media timelines, chat message history, and infinite-scroll mobile feeds.

interviewTip: When asked to design a feed or message history endpoint, immediately specify cursor pagination over offset pagination: 'We will use cursor-based pagination backed by a composite index on `(created_at, id)`. This prevents duplicate feed items as new posts arrive and maintains sub-10ms lookup times even on deep pages.'
